Girls U15 Rep Team coach Terry Duff was on the ice on Oct. 31 helping out with World Girls’ Ice Hockey Weekend. “Hockey is for everybody,” Terry Duff recently told a group of young female hockey players in Williams Lake, encouraging them to believe in themselves, work hard and always try their best. “Girls can do anything anyone can do.” Duff’s words of empowerment came after more than 40 girls from U7 through U15 hit the ice on Saturday, Oct. 31 at the Cariboo Memorial Recreation Complex to celebrate World Girls’ Ice Hockey Weekend. According to Hockey Canada, the International Ice Hockey Federation has united countries around the world since 2011 for World Girls’ Ice Hockey Weekend events aimed to retain, recruit and engage players, coaches, officials and fans of all ages. In Williams Lake Duff was one of the coaches helping lead the day that included a number of drills, activities and games. “We have a big increase in girls hockey, and hopefully with somebody like myself who is really advocating to get the girls on the ice and have all these ice times the numbers will increase even more,” said Williams Lake Minor Hockey Association female coordinator Courtney Petryshen, noting the girls U18 Rep Team could not make the day being away in Prince George for weekend games. Duff has more than 15 years of hockey coaching and teaching experience having gotten involved since his daughters wanted to play. This year he coaches the girls U15 Rep Team that includes players from Quesnel and 100 Mile House.

It’s a simple activity on its face, yet it’s one that has created countless connections across the millennia. That age-old tradition has been carried on at the Canadian Mental Health Association South Cariboo Branch with its new weekly Soups On! Free Friday Soup Program. Our first couple, we had five people and we have had up to nine people eat in and have soup with us. With Halloween falling on a Saturday, it was initially unclear if the annual festivities would be a go as many businesses, including professional services and government agencies, are closed on weekends. For years Douillard has organized the Downtown Trick r Treat annual festivities with her mother, Joan. She personally likes the 2 p.m. start time which is quiet, providing the perfect opportunity for toddlers, kids with sensory or sensitivity issues and anyone who might get overwhelmed to trick-or-treat before things pick up. She remembers the first Downtown Trick r Treat with about 15 locations signed up and running to Safeway to buy whatever she could to drop off after they ran out of candy in just 15 minutes. The biggest year for handing out candy at the Realm of Toys was before COVID with 744 kids. “After COVID we definitely saw a huge drop in numbers and it’s only slowly been increasing,” Douillard said, adding last year they hit over 500. items.title: [globalnews.ca] Carney sets six December byelections, giving Liberals chance to widen majority
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called federal byelections for Dec. 7 in six ridings across Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan: Scarborough North and Brantford—Brant South in Ontario, and Yorkton—Melville in Saskatchewan. The three Quebec contests are Laurier—Sainte-Marie, Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton. The races will fill vacancies left by MPs from several parties. The Liberals hold 173 of the House of Commons’ 343 seats. Winning any of the vacant ridings would increase that total, although losing all six would not cost them the ability to govern. In Brantford—Brant South, Conservative nominee and Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis faces Liberal Joy O’Donnell and independent candidate Dave Carroll, who had sought the Conservative nomination. Advance voting is scheduled for Nov. 27-30, with special ballots available before Dec. 1.

items.content_html:

A study of more than 100,000 UK Biobank participants found that a 1972 British law requiring teenagers to stay in school until 16 was associated with fewer diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias nearly 50 years later. Using the reform’s September 1, 1957, birth-date cutoff, researchers compared people subject to different school-leaving rules and reported a 0.88% reduction in dementia incidence among those affected. Researchers also found the reduction among participants with high genetic susceptibility. They cautioned that dementia was uncommon in this cohort, whose diagnoses were tracked only through age 65, making the estimate imprecise. Protesters blamed corruption and failures of oversight, accusations the government rejected. The movement’s anti-corruption campaign drew support beyond students, and it entered the election with a slate of civil society candidates. With final results still pending, the Student List faces the task of forming a government without a single established leader. Its candidates have limited political experience. European Union officials offered help with rule-of-law and media reforms, while Vučić alleged foreign interference without providing evidence.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

items.title: [firstpost.com] Brazil markets slide as Lula win revives fiscal concerns
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Brazil-linked assets fell in early offshore trading Monday after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. Investors had favored Bolsonaro, whom they viewed as more likely to pursue fiscal austerity and deregulation. An exchange-traded fund tracking Brazilian equities fell as much as 16% in Japan, while the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF dropped nearly 20% in overnight trading; currency derivatives signaled a possible decline of more than 10% in the real. These were early offshore moves, not Brazilian closing prices. Brazil’s electoral court gave Lula 51.79% of the vote to Bolsonaro’s 48.21%. Lula’s next term begins in January 2027. Public debt reached 82.9% of GDP in August, up more than 10 percentage points during Lula’s current term, while less than 8% of the federal budget is adjustable. Lula has pledged to protect social spending and raise the minimum wage. Investors are watching whether he can meet those pledges while stabilizing debt and inflation. Brazil’s benchmark interest rate was 13.75% and inflation was 4.6%. Inflation is not expected to reach the central bank’s 3% target until as late as 2029, Reuters reported. A consumption-tax overhaul approved in 2023 is also due to take effect in January, but the government has not disclosed its effective rate; independent analysts estimate it at about 28%.

AI companies and lawmakers are proposing tighter controls after agents breached testing boundaries and accessed outside systems. Oversight proposals have also entered U.S. election debates. Anthropic wants regulators to seek court orders blocking models judged dangerous; OpenAI instead backs enforceable shutdown controls operated by developers, independent assessments and broader incident reporting. The companies also differ over whether regulators should be able to suspend deployment or rely on company-run safeguards. New York lawmakers proposed expanding safety reporting, requiring independent audits and giving the state authority to restrict computing used for high-risk development, while California officials are weighing changes to existing rules. California’s governor has directed officials to submit recommendations by Nov. 16; a state hearing on Oct. 28 focused on incidents that current law may not require companies to report. President Trump has favored voluntary, “morally binding” industry controls and argued that stricter rules could weaken U.S. competition with China. Polling in Ohio and Iowa found strong support for a range of safety measures, and local opposition to data centers has led to ballot measures in dozens of U.S. jurisdictions. The White House says it seeks both American leadership and consumer protection.
